title: Design Food Rating System
description: Design a system tracking the highest-rated food per cuisine under rating changes, using a per-cuisine max-heap with lazy deletion.

blocks.text: Design a FoodRatings class initialized with parallel arrays foods, cuisines, and ratings. Support changeRating(food, newRating), which updates a food's rating, and highestRated(cuisine), which returns the highest-rated food of that cuisine, breaking ties by lexicographically smaller name.

blocks.caption: Each cuisine keeps its own priority structure; stale entries left behind by rating changes are discarded lazily.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Constructor","foods[], cuisines[], ratings[] (all length n, food names unique)"],["changeRating(food, newRating)","Updates that food's current rating"],["highestRated(cuisine)","Returns the name of the top-rated food in that cuisine, ties broken by smaller name"],["Goal","Both operations should run efficiently even with many calls"]]}

blocks.text: Needing the "current maximum" repeatedly, with values that can change over time, is the classic signal for a max-heap (priority queue) per group. Since a heap does not support efficient direct updates, the standard workaround is lazy deletion: push a NEW entry on every rating change instead of updating in place, and when querying, discard stale entries (whose stored rating no longer matches the food's current rating) from the top until a valid one is found.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: The same lazy-deletion-via-a-source-of-truth-map pattern used in Design a Number Container System, applied here per cuisine group instead of per value.

Picture a leaderboard for each cuisine, showing the highest-rated dish. When a dish's rating changes, rather than editing the leaderboard entry directly (which a heap cannot do efficiently), a new entry is posted, leaving the old one behind as outdated. When someone checks the leaderboard, outdated entries at the top are cleared away until the true current leader is revealed.

blocks.caption: Stale leaderboard entries are cleared lazily, only when someone actually checks the top.

items: A max-heap per cuisine, ordered by (rating descending, name ascending), always has the TRUE current leader somewhere near the top, though possibly buried under stale entries.
A food-to-current-rating map is the single source of truth; a heap entry is valid only if its stored rating matches this map.
changeRating simply pushes a new heap entry; the old entry becomes naturally stale and gets cleaned up whenever it is eventually encountered at the top.

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: After sushi's rating changes to 16, it becomes the new top of the japanese heap since 16 exceeds every other japanese rating, and the stale (8, sushi) entry simply sits deeper in the heap, never reached because the valid (16, sushi) entry is found first.

A brute-force approach keeps, for each cuisine, a set of its food names and scans all of them on every highestRated call to find the current maximum by consulting a food-to-rating map directly. This is correct and simple but linear in the cuisine's size per query.

A max-heap per cuisine speeds up finding the maximum, but heaps cannot efficiently update an existing entry's priority. The standard fix is lazy deletion: every changeRating pushes a brand new entry rather than modifying an old one, and highestRated pops stale entries (rating mismatch against the source-of-truth map) off the top until a valid one surfaces, which is exactly the current top since the heap is still correctly ordered otherwise.
Track a set of food names per cuisine and a food-to-rating map. On highestRated, scan every food in that cuisine's set to find the best (rating, name) pair directly.

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: A cuisine with many foods pays a full linear scan on every single highestRated call, even when ratings rarely change between queries.

Give each cuisine a max-heap ordered by (rating descending, name ascending). changeRating pushes a fresh entry with the new rating, in O(log m). highestRated pops any stale entries (whose stored rating no longer matches the food-to-rating map) from the top, then returns the food at the now-valid top; the total amortized cost across all pops, over the whole run, is bounded by the total number of pushes, since each entry is popped at most once.

items: Maintain foodToCuisine and foodToRating as the sources of truth.
Each cuisine has its own heap ordered by rating descending, name ascending for tie-breaking.
changeRating: update the rating map, push a new heap entry. highestRated: lazily discard stale top entries, then return the valid top.

items: Lazy deletion turns an update-unfriendly heap into an efficient priority structure: push new, invalidate old, clean up only when actually queried.
A hash map tracking "current truth" alongside the heap is what makes stale entries detectable.
Grouping heaps by category (here, cuisine) is a common way to answer "the best within this group" queries efficiently.

blocks.text: Design Food Rating System uses a max-heap per cuisine, ordered by rating descending and name ascending for ties, combined with lazy deletion: rating changes push fresh entries rather than updating in place, and queries discard stale entries from the top before returning the current leader. This gives fast amortized performance for both operations without needing a heap that supports direct priority updates.
